18                                 NOTICE OF REMOVAL
19   TO THE CLERK OF THE ABOVE-ENTITLED COURT:
20         PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that Defendant TESLA, INC. (incorrectly named
21   herein as Tesla Motors, Inc. [“Tesla”]), by its counsel, ROSEWALDORF LLP, hereby
22   removes to this Court, pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332, 1441 and 1446, based upon
23   diversity of citizenship, the claims pending as Case No. 24-CVI-07020 of the Superior
24   Court of California, County of San Mateo. In support of this removal, Tesla states as
25   follows:
26   ///
27   ///
28
                                                 1
                              DEFENDANT TESLA INC.’S NOTICE OF REMOVAL
             Case 3:24-cv-08973-TSH        Document 1     Filed 12/11/24   Page 2 of 8




 1                                 I.     THE REMOVED CASE
 2         1.        The removed case is a civil action commenced in the Superior Court of
 3   California, County of Orange, by Plaintiff OSCAR ROSALES (“Plaintiff”) against
 4   TESLA, INC., entitled OSCAR vs. TESLA MOTORS, INC.; and DOES 1 through 100,
 5   Case No. 24-CIV-07020 (the “State Action”). The only named Defendant is Tesla.
 6         2.        Plaintiff filed the State Action on November 7, 2024, asserting claims
 7   against Defendant Tesla for violation of California’s Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty
 8   Act (“Song-Beverly”) and for negligent repair (Compl., Exhibit “A” to the Declaration
 9   of Mark W. Skanes [“Skanes Decl.”], served and filed herewith.)
10         3.        Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332, a federal district court will have original
11   jurisdiction over all “civil actions where the matter in controversy exceeds the sum or
12   value of $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs, and is between – (1) citizens of
13   different States . . . .” A corporation is deemed a citizen of “every State and foreign state
14   by which it has been incorporated and of the State or foreign state where it has its
15   principal place of business.” 28 U.S.C. § 1332(c).
16                         II.      PROCEDURAL REQUIREMENTS
17         4.        Generally, a defendant has thirty (30) days after receipt by the defendant,
18   through service or otherwise, of a copy of an amended pleading, motion, order or other
19   paper from which it may first be ascertained that the case is one which is or has become
20   removable. 28 U.S.C § 1446(b)(3).
21         5.        Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1446(a), copies of all process, pleadings, and
22   orders for the State Action in Tesla’s possession are contained in Exhibits A–D filed
23   herewith. (Skanes Decl. ¶¶ 5–8).
24         6.        Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1446(a), venue is proper in the Northern District
25   of California because this district embraces the place in which the State Action has been
26   pending.
27   ///
28
                                                    2
                                 DEFENDANT TESLA INC.’S NOTICE OF REMOVAL
               Case 3:24-cv-08973-TSH          Document 1     Filed 12/11/24    Page 3 of 8




 1            7.           Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1446(d), a true and correct copy of this Notice
 2   of Removal will be filed with the Superior Court of California, County of San Mateo,
 3   promptly after filing of same in this Court.
 4            8.           Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1446(d), written notice of filing of this Notice of
 5   Removal will be given to all adverse parties promptly after the filing of same in this
 6   Court.
 7            9.           If any question arises as to the propriety of the removal of this action,
 8   Tesla requests the opportunity to conduct discovery, brief any disputed issues and to
 9   present oral argument in favor of its position that this case is properly removable.
10            10.          Nothing in this Notice of Removal shall be interpreted as a waiver or
11   relinquishment of Tesla’s right to assert defenses including, without limitation, the
12   defenses of (i) lack of jurisdiction over person, (ii) improper venue and/or forum non
13   conveniens, (iii) insufficiency of process, (iv) insufficiency of service of process, (v)
14   improper joinder of claims and/or parties, (vi) failure to state a claim, (vii) failure to join
15   indispensable party(ies), or (viii) any other procedural or substantive defenses available
16   under state or federal law.
17                  III.    THE AMOUNT IN CONTROVERSY FOR DIVERSITY
18                                        JURISDICTION IS MET
19            11.          The amount in controversy in this action exceeds $75,000, exclusive of
20   interest and costs. See 28 U.S.C. § 1332.
21            12.          The removing party’s initial burden is to “file a notice of removal that
22   includes ‘a plausible allegation that the amount in controversy exceeds the jurisdictional
23   threshold.’” Ibarra v. Manheim Invs., Inc., 775 F.3d 1193, 1195 (9th Cir. 2015) (quoting
24   Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Co., LLC v. Owens, 135 S.Ct. 547, 554 (2014)). “By
25   design, § 1446(a) tracks the general pleading requirement stated in Rule 8(a)” which
26   requires only that the grounds for removal be stated in a “short and plain statement.”
27   Dart, supra, at 553.
28
                                                       3
                                    DEFENDANT TESLA INC.’S NOTICE OF REMOVAL
             Case 3:24-cv-08973-TSH       Document 1      Filed 12/11/24    Page 4 of 8




 1         13.        Generally, a federal district court will first “consider whether it is
 2   ‘facially apparent’ from the complaint that the jurisdictional amount is in controversy.”
 3   Abrego v. Dow Chem. Co., 443 F.3d 676, 690 (9th Cir. 2006) (internal citation omitted).
 4   A defendant may remove a suit to federal court notwithstanding the failure of the
 5   plaintiff to plead the required amount. Absent the facial showing from the complaint,
 6   the court may consider facts averred in the removal petition. Id. Next, if the defendant’s
 7   allegation(s) regarding the amount in controversy is challenged, then “both sides submit
 8   proof and the court decides, by a preponderance of the evidence, whether the amount-
 9   in-controversy requirement has been satisfied.” Ibarra, supra, at 1195. At that time, “it
10   may be appropriate to allow discovery relevant to [the] jurisdictional amount prior to
11   remanding.” Abrego, supra, at 691. (internal citation omitted).
12         14.        Tesla disputes that it is liable for any damages whatsoever to Plaintiff.
13   Nevertheless, Tesla can demonstrate that the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000
14   under the “preponderance of the evidence” standard. See Guglielmino v. McKee Foods
15   Corp., 506 F.3d 696, 699 (9th Cir. 2007). The standard requires only that the removing
16   party present evidence that “it is more likely than not” that the amount in controversy is
17   satisfied. Id.
18         15.    In the Complaint, Plaintiff seeks monetary relief. Plaintiff asserts claims
19   for breach of express and implied warranties and violation of the Song-Beverly
20   Consumer Warranty Act (Cal. Civ. Code § 1790 et seq.) based upon alleged defects in a
21   Tesla Model 3 along with a claim for negligent repair (see Compl., generally).
22         16.    Plaintiff seeks rescission of the sales contract, restitution, civil penalties “in
23   a sum twice the amount of actual damages,” consequential and incidental damages,
24   general damages, reasonable attorney’s fees and costs, along with pre-judgment and
25   post-judgment interest (Compl., Prayer). See Cal.Civ. Code §§ 1793.2, 1794(b)(2). see
26   also Cal.Civ.Code § 1794(c).
27         17.    Where, like here, a claim is asserted under the Song-Beverly Warranty Act,
28   the court may consider actual damages and civil penalties under the Song-Beverly
                                                  4
                               DEFENDANT TESLA INC.’S NOTICE OF REMOVAL
                Case 3:24-cv-08973-TSH                Document 1           Filed 12/11/24         Page 5 of 8




 1   Warranty Act in determining the amount in controversy. See Brady v. Mercedes-Benz
 2   USA, Inc., 243 F.Supp.2d 1004, 1009 (N.D.Cal. 2002). Moreover, this Court may also
 3   consider reasonable estimates of attorneys’ fees in calculating the amount in
 4   controversy. See Alvarado v. TESLA LLC, 2017 WL 2495495 (C.D.Cal. 2017), citing
 5   Galt G/S v. JSS Scandinavia, 142 F.3d 1150, 1155-1156 (9th Cir. 1998); Guglielmino v.
 6   McKee Foods Corp., 506 F.3d 696, 699-700 (9th Cir. 2007). The Song-Beverly Act
 7   allows for the recovery of attorneys’ fees, which commonly exceed $25,000 (Skanes
 8   Decl. ¶ 12).
 9            18.      As alleged in the Complaint, in connection with their claims under Song-
10   Beverly, Plaintiff seeks reimbursement of the price paid, restitution damages, incidental
11   and consequential damages, and reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs (Compl., Prayer).
12   Therefore, Plaintiff is allegedly seeking a minimum of $43,491.96 restitution which is
13   calculated as the total amount paid for the vehicle ($44,178.41 (see Retail Installment
14   Contract, Line 5, Exhibit “E” to Skanes Decl.), finance charges of $4,468 (paid to date
15   of a total $12,096.23 total finance charges), and less a reasonable allowance for use in
16   the amount of $5,154.45. 1 See Cal.Civ.Code § 1793.2(d)(2)(B).
17            19.      A civil penalty of two times the claimed actual damages would equal
18   $86,983.92. Taken together, Plaintiff’s claims for actual damages and civil penalties
19   equals $129,535.23, even before considering unspecified incidental and consequential
20   damages that Plaintiff seeks in this matter. See Kirzhner v. Mercedes-Benz USA, LLC,
21   9 Cal. 5th 966 (holding that a consumer is entitled to recover incidental damages under
22   Civ Code § 1794 if they were incurred and paid as a result of a manufacturer’s failure to
23   promptly provide a replacement vehicle or restitution under Song-Beverly, including the
24   costs of registration and renewal).
25

26
     1
       Defendant anticipates that Plaintiff will argue the first attempted repair occurred on February 21, 2024 at 15,607 miles.
27   Therefore, the mileage offset would equal $5,154.45 calculated by taking 15,592 miles (the mileage at the first alleged repair
     less the 15 miles at delivery) divided by 120,000 multiplied by the purchase price of $39,670.00 (Retail Installment Sales
28   Contract, Line 1.A, Ex. “E” to Skanes Decl.).
                                                                     5
                                        DEFENDANT TESLA INC.’S NOTICE OF REMOVAL
             Case 3:24-cv-08973-TSH        Document 1      Filed 12/11/24    Page 6 of 8




 1         20.    Furthermore, Plaintiff is also seeking attorneys’ fees, which commonly
 2   exceed $25,000 in Song Beverly cases (Skanes Decl., ¶ 12).
 3         21.    Based upon the foregoing, Defendant has demonstrated that the total
 4   amount in controversy exceeds $75,000 and removal is proper.
 5         22.    Independent from Defendant’s showing above, Plaintiff’s own allegations
 6   demonstrate that the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. Specifically, Plaintiff
 7   alleges they seeks at least $25,001 in actual damages (see Complaint at ¶ 15). This
 8   alleged amount is in addition to the civil penalty they seek that equals $50,002 (i.e., “two
 9   times” the alleged actual damages of $25,001). Importantly, according to Plaintiff’s own
10   allegations, there is no question that they are entitled to this full “two times” civil penalty
11   based upon the allegation that Tesla’s failure to comply with the statute was “willful”
12   (see Complaint ¶ 18). Moreover, Plaintiff seeks incidental damages and attorneys’ fees
13   (see Compl. Prayer).
14         23.    Accordingly, on the face of the Complaint and by Plaintiff’s own
15   allegations, they are “entitled” to both $25,001 in actual damages and a full “two times”
16   that amount (an additional $50,002) as a civil penalty.
17         24.    Based on the foregoing, Defendant has demonstrated by both a detailed
18   calculation and independently by the face of the Complaint, that the amount in
19   controversy exceeds $75,000 even without considering attorneys’ fees. At the very least,
20   unless Plaintiff concedes that these allegations are frivolous, Plaintiff is estopped from
21   arguing that the amount in controversy has not been met.
22                          IV.    COMPLETE DIVERSITY EXISTS
23         25.       The basic requirement in diversity cases is that all plaintiffs be of
24   different citizenship than all defendants. Any instance of common citizenship prevents
25   federal diversity jurisdiction. For diversity purposes, a natural person is a “citizen” of
26   the state which he or she is domiciled. See Kantor v. Wellesley Galleries, Ltd., 704 F.2d
27   1088, 1090 (9th Cir. 1983). A natural person's domicile is the place he or she resides
28   with the intention to remain or to which he or she intends to return. See Kanter v.
                                                  6
                               DEFENDANT TESLA INC.’S NOTICE OF REMOVAL
             Case 3:24-cv-08973-TSH      Document 1     Filed 12/11/24    Page 7 of 8




 1   Warner-Lambert Co., 265 F.3d. 853, 857 (9th Cir. 2001). A party’s residence is prima
 2   facie evidence of domicile, and only if that party disputes domicile is the removing party
 3   required to provide proof of domiciliary intent. See, e.g., State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co.
 4   v. Dyer, 19 F.3d 514, 520 (10th Cir. 1994).
 5         26.      A corporation, on the other hand, is deemed to be a citizen of any State
 6   by which it has been incorporated and of the State where it has its principal place of
 7   business. See 28 U.S.C. §1332(c)(1). A corporation’s principal place of business refers
 8   to the place where its high-level officers “direct, control, and coordinate the
 9   corporation's activities.” See Hertz Corp. v. Friend, 559 U.S. 77, 92-93 (2010). “[T]he
10   citizenship of an LLC for purposes of the diversity jurisdiction is the citizenship of its
11   members.” Cosgrove v. Bartolotta, 150 F.3d 729, 731 (7th Cir. 1998) cited by Johnson
12   v. Columbia Properties Anchorage, LP, 437 F.3d 894, 899 (9th Cir. 2006) and GMAC
13   Comm'l Credit LLC v. Dillard Dept. Stores, Inc., 357 F.3d 827, 829 (8th Cir. 2004).
14         27.      A case is removable on diversity grounds if diversity of citizenship can
15   be ascertained from the face of Plaintiff’s Complaint or this fact is disclosed in
16   pleadings, motions or papers “from which it may first be ascertained that the case is one
17   which is or has become removable . . ..” See 28 U.S.C. §1446(b)(3).
18         28.      As noted above, a party’s residence is prima facie evidence of domicile,
19   and only if that party disputes domicile is the removing party required to provide proof
20   of domiciliary intent. See, e.g., State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co. v. Dyer, 19 F.3d 514, 520
21   (10th Cir. 1994). “It is assumed … that a person’s current residence is also his domicile.”
22   13E Charles Alan Wright & Arthur R. Miller, Federal Practice & Procedure §3612 (3d.
23   ed. 2013).
24         29.       Plaintiff is and was at the time of filing of the Complaint, a citizen and
25   resident of California. (Compl., ¶ 2, see also Skanes Decl., ¶ 9 & Exhibit “E”
26   [demonstrating Plaintiff’s domicile in San Mateo County]; Ervin v. Ballard Marine
27   Constr., Inc., No. 16-cv-02931-WHO, 2016 WL 4239710, at *3-4 (N.D.Cal. 2016)
28   [internal citations omitted] (Plaintiff’s complaint stated only that he was a resident of
                                                 7
                              DEFENDANT TESLA INC.’S NOTICE OF REMOVAL
               Case 3:24-cv-08973-TSH     Document 1      Filed 12/11/24   Page 8 of 8




 1   Oregon, it made no statement as to Plaintiff’s citizenship. The Court found that for
 2   diversity purposes a plaintiff is a citizen of the state in which he or she resides in the
 3   absence of evidence to the contrary.)).
 4            30.   Tesla is, and was at the time Plaintiff commenced this action, incorporated
 5   under Texas law with its principal place of business in Texas.
 6            31.     Accordingly, diversity existed between Plaintiff and Tesla as of the time
 7   this action was filed, as well as the date of this notice. See Salveson v. Western State
 8   Bank Card Assn., 731 F.2d 1423 (9th Cir. 1984).
 9                                     V.      CONCLUSION
10            29.   The State Action may be removed to this Court by Tesla in accordance with
11   the provisions of 28 U.S.C. § 1441 because: (i) this action is a civil action pending within
12   the jurisdiction of the United States District Court for the Northern District of California,
13   (ii) the action involves diversity jurisdiction because the parties are citizens of different
14   states, and (iii) the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000.00 exclusive of interest and
15   costs.
16   Dated: December 11, 2024                              ROSEWALDORF LLP
17
                                                 By:/s/Mark W Skanes
